name: Paternalistic conservatism
scope: The strand of conservatism in which those with authority, wealth or privilege take moral responsibility for protecting the poorer and weaker, in order to keep order, social cohesion and existing institutions, and to head off Marxist revolution (Gjorshoski 2016, 'Paternalistic conservatism'). Its sources give Burke as an early writer, Disraeli's Toryism as its 'purest form' and Bismarck's 1880s compulsory insurance laws as the continental case, and add the later Anglo-Saxon and Western European conservative parties' social protection, Keynesian full-employment policy, corporatist partnership in firms and agricultural support. The source calls its motive 'more pragmatic than idealistic'. Excludes the neoliberal, neoconservative and Christian-democratic variants the same source treats separately, and one-nation conservatism, Red Toryism, Tory democracy or other ideologies' sources, which are not used here.

sources.title: The Ideological Specifics of the Variants of Contemporary Conservatism (section 'Paternalistic Conservatism')
sources.author: Nikola Gjorshoski, Journal of Liberty and International Affairs 2(1), 2016
sources.usedFor: Defines paternalistic conservatism: origins, Disraeli, Bismarck's insurance laws, unified nation, partnership and corporatism, agriculture

notes: Phase 1 (scope). Only one defining source naming the ideology was found open: Gjorshoski 2016. The SEP 'Conservatism' entry, EBSCO and tutor2u pages saved in the source folder discuss one-nation conservatism or conservatism and never name paternalistic conservatism, so are not cited. Andrew Heywood's Political Ideologies (2007, 2012), Vincent 2009 and Dorey 1995, which Wikipedia cites, are lending-only. The two downloaded books are not used: Heywood, Samuel, High church politics (1792) is a different author from Andrew Heywood and is about test-act disputes; Steinberg, Bismarck: A Life never uses the name or 'paternalistic' (checked by grep), so it is a biography of one person, a coatrack for the ideology. Key figures: Disraeli (a key figure of one-nation-conservatism) and Burke (of conservatism) are named by the source but belong to those ideologies, so none is listed. Answers: only Gjorshoski (s5) defines the ideology under its name, so answers rest on it alone and most statements are null. Themes searched in it: welfare and social insurance, class relations, nation and patriotism, corporatism and firms, agriculture, state and revolution, pragmatism, hierarchy. The earlier pass's answers rested on Wikipedia, the SEP entry on conservatism and Disraeli's 1872 Crystal Palace speech, none of which are a defining source naming the ideology; they are changed or nulled. Wikipedia's cited works not opened: Heywood 2007 and 2012, Vincent 2009 and Dorey 1995 (lending-only copies).

class-collaboration.rationale: Gjorshoski ('Social protection mechanisms for workers') describes cooperation and collaboration between groups, rather than antagonism and division, as the practice characteristic of all periods of paternalistic rule, and ('Loyalty, partnership and corporatism') calls for relationships of trust and partnership among all participants in production.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Gjorshoski ('The concept of unified nation') says the state is present in all categories and every member of the nation has the right to live in welfare, with guaranteed jobs, good wages, education and healthcare named as what binds people to the nation.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Gjorshoski ('Loyalty, partnership and corporatism') describes the economic logic as a welfare state with a reduction of income disparities 'but not to the extreme' and a moderate hierarchy, so it aims to narrow gaps rather than equalise outcomes.

farm-price-support.rationale: Gjorshoski ('Special care to agriculture') says paternalism is most evident in agrarian policy, whose principles include production subsidies and intervention purchases when markets are disrupted.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Gjorshoski ('The concept of unified nation') reports the claim that established institutions such as the monarch, parliament and the Anglican Church can be preserved only if the working class votes Conservative, treating their preservation as the aim.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Gjorshoski describes compulsory social insurance, a welfare state and state-supported social protection as the doctrine's practice ('Social protection mechanisms for workers', 'Loyalty, partnership and corporatism'), which goes beyond protecting people from violence alone.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Gjorshoski's section 'Paternalistic Conservatism' bases the doctrine on the principle that those who hold authority take moral responsibility for protecting those who are worse off, and the section 'The concept of unified nation' says the wealthy and privileged bear responsibility and obligations to the poorer and less powerful.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Gjorshoski (section 'Paternalistic Conservatism') says the underlying motive of its social action is 'more pragmatic than idealistic', and that pragmatism is a primary determinant of conservative parties' activities.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Gjorshoski ('Social protection mechanisms for workers') says the conservative answer to the Marxist call for violent revolution was affirmative action to improve workers' position, 'not through violent methods', and ('The concept of unified nation') gives the doctrine's slogan as 'change to preserve existing'.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Gjorshoski ('The concept of unified nation') gives the doctrine's stance as 'change to preserve existing' and says conservative values such as tradition, authority and order are secured by policies fitted to practical circumstances, with established institutions kept.

social-market-economy.rationale: Gjorshoski ('Loyalty, partnership and corporatism') describes a balance between individualism and collectivism that keeps innovation and entrepreneurship while building a welfare state and social protection mechanisms for workers ('Social protection mechanisms for workers').

state-harmful.rationale: Gjorshoski ('Social protection mechanisms for workers') presents the doctrine as the conservative answer to Marxism's aim of repealing the state and the existing order, and describes paternalism as authority exercised to protect the worse off, with the state present in all categories ('The concept of unified nation').

workers-nation.rationale: Gjorshoski ('The concept of unified nation') says conservatives promoting the unified nation fostered loyalty and patriotism among workers, countering the socialist idea that workers had no state of their own.

summary: Paternalistic conservatism, as Gjorshoski describes it, holds that those with authority and means have a moral responsibility to protect the weaker and poorer, from motives that are more pragmatic than idealistic: keeping order, social cohesion and existing institutions and heading off Marxist revolution. In practice it means social protection for workers (Bismarck's compulsory insurance), a unified nation held together by welfare and patriotism, partnership between classes and corporatist cooperation in firms, and care for agriculture, while keeping a market economy and a moderate hierarchy.
